transcript: Whenever I feel discouraged about the state of musical theatre on Broadway right now, I just think of 1995. And if you're not aware, in the 1995 Tony season, a total of five musicals opened up. Just five. And three of them were revivals. So for Best New Musical, there were only two eligible candidates. Smokey Joe's Cafe, a jukebox musical, and Sunset Boulevard, a movie adaptation. The the internet's least favourite sub genres. So few musicals opened up that season that more musicals closed from previous seasons in that year. And then literally the next season, rent comes along and changes the game. Rent is not just one of those once in a generation defining musicals that's just so good and so new and fresh that it kind of invigorates the entire industry and changes the future of musical theatre. But rent also changed the way that, like, we sold tickets. Rent literally invented the in person rush. And then that demand for that was so high, they transformed it into an in person lottery. Like. Like, that was rent. We have those things because of rent. Like, if you weren't alive during this time, I don't know if you realise how huge rent was, but there was literally an episode of wings on network television that was all about the characters trying to get tickets to rent. Like, that's how big this show was. And I feel in my bones that we are due for that level of A seismic shift. And rent wasn't the last one. That was arguably Hamilton. But rent is maybe the largest jump from, like, such a bleak season as 1995 to 1996. In my heart of hearts, I truly believe that the show to do it next is going to be a show that embraces digital accessibility. I truly, truly, truly believe that is going to be our next shift in the industry. But that it's going to make audiences come to theatre in a way that they haven't before. That people are going to be craving live experiences like they crave live concerts, they're going to be craving live storytelling and live performance. And that in order to get them into that building, we are going to have to embrace digital, uh, in a way that we're starting to see. We're starting to see.
